source.title: Tool Specifications Matter: Uncovering and Mitigating Safety Risks in AI Agents
source.authors: Minghui Pan; Jiayuxuan Yang; Yuan-Yuan Yuan; Yu Jiang; Zhen-Peng Chen

record.file_problem: none noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Uses a refusal-direction extraction and projection analysis based on prior work, but does not ablate or add the harmful-minus-benign refusal direction. Its causal intervention targets a different vector, the schema-versus-text direction, and its safeguard results do not test the claimed refusal-direction mechanism.
record.gate_note: The paper measures refusal-direction AUROC under agent-context changes and reports refusal behavior, schema-direction analyses, and steering outcomes. These bear on agent safety and refusal-related representations but do not test the claim versions as stated: in particular, steering is against the schema direction, not the claimed refusal direction. SafeKeep benchmark comparisons are its own safeguard evaluation, not tests that attacks suppress the refusal direction, so they are not included as claim rows. No values used only for method or parameter selection are included.
record.test_reason: The study uses the difference-in-means refusal direction from the original paper as a fixed diagnostic probe. It reports harmful–benign AUROC and projections under chatbot vs. agent inputs. It never ablates or adds the refusal direction. Its causal steering uses a separate schema-vs-flattened-text direction. Its jailbreak-type results (InjecAgent) evaluate its own safeguard, not suppression of the refusal direction. The agent-context findings concern separability along the direction, a related but different construct, so they go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that schema-formatted tool specifications induce a hidden-state direction opposing refusal, weaken refusal-related separation, and causally contribute to harmful tool execution. SafeKeep, which judges safety on flattened specifications, raises average refusal from 23.8% to 70.6% and cuts injection ASR from 25.6% to 2.5% while preserving task handling.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses the prior refusal-direction extraction/projection approach for diagnosis, but defines and steers a different direction: the average hidden-state change between schema-formatted and flattened tool specifications. It does not reproduce the original refusal-direction ablation or addition procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured separability varies with input configuration, especially when tool specifications are added; representation conversion and semantic randomization also yield different AUROCs. Schema-direction steering outcomes vary with alpha, with invalid outputs rising sharply at alpha 8 and reaching 100.0% at alpha 12.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding agent context, chiefly schema-formatted tool specifications, lowers harmful–benign AUROC along a fixed chatbot-derived refusal direction in three models (e.g. Llama 0.927→0.740). Flattening the schemas largely restores it; randomizing their semantics does not. Llama refusal also drops from 58% to 3%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The chatbot-derived refusal direction's harmful–benign separation degrades under schema-formatted tool contexts, alongside reduced behavioural refusal in agents.

fits_no_version.finding: In Llama3.1-8B, the harmful-request schema direction is anti-aligned with the refusal direction at all layers. Subtracting it at alpha=4 raises refusal from 5% to 47.5%, but larger alpha mostly yields invalid outputs (77.5% at alpha=8, 100% at alpha=12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An input-format-induced direction anti-aligned with the refusal direction causally suppresses refusal in agent contexts.

record.problems: The mechanistic behavioral steering results are reported for Llama3.1-8B-Instruct only. The schema-direction intervention also produces substantial invalid outputs at higher strengths. Numerical layerwise values for the cosine and first-token projection plots are not stated in the text. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the tabulated results.
record.rows_left_out: SafeKeep and baseline benchmark comparisons in Table 4 and Sections 6.4–6.5 were left out because they evaluate the paper's safeguard rather than whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or whether the claimed direction mediates refusal. No other claim-relevant results were omitted.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of the harmful-minus-harmless direction; no capability-preservation test under such interventions.
Does not test whether prompt injections or jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction; no training against its ablation.
No test of affine, cone or multi-direction refusal structure.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal.
No transfer across languages, model variants or base-to-instruct stages. Transfer across input formats (chatbot to agent) is measured only as separability, not causally.
No comparison of training methods or stages.
No reasoning-model analysis; Qwen3-8B is used without a reasoning-mode analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The refusal direction serves only as a probe; the original paper is cited as [3]. The steering evidence covers one model (Llama3.1-8B), and alpha 8–12 mainly produces invalid output. SafeKeep results (Table 4) are correctly excluded as evaluations of the paper's own method. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No removal or addition of the harmful-minus-benign refusal direction; no test of its causal mediation of refusal or of preservation of other abilities under its ablation.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration test.
Prompt injection is evaluated, but the paper does not test whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.

The schema direction is analyzed as a distinct, complementary input-format effect; the paper does not test whether refusal itself is better described by an affine set, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision is tested.
Multiple LLMs are used for some evaluations, but transfer of the claimed refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages is not tested.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or training stages.
No test of the claim in reasoning models.
